title: Social and economic rights fulfillment is measured against feasible capacity, exposing delivery gaps that GDP alone hides
source_unit: University of Connecticut Social and Economic Rights Empowerment Initiative, 2026 International SERF Index update
geography: Up to 200 countries, with separate low/middle-income and high-income assessment standards and sex-disaggregated rights indicators

denominator.unit: countries with at least one right or component-right series available

rights_domains.value: The index evaluates five rights: health, education, food, housing, and work

time_span.unit: years covered by the updated international series

capacity_benchmark.value: Achievement Possibility Frontiers benchmark rights enjoyment against the best observed performance at comparable per-capita income levels

interpretation.value: The frame shifts evaluation from resources alone to whether states achieve the rights outcomes feasible at their level of resources

observations.method: The SERF methodology combines socioeconomic outcome indicators with per-capita income and Achievement Possibility Frontiers to estimate the percentage of feasible rights fulfillment achieved by each country.
observations.uncertainty: A score of 100% means performance matches the historically best observed benchmark at that income level; it does not mean universal rights enjoyment. Composite scores depend on indicator availability, modelling choices, aggregation, and benchmark construction.
observations.subgroup: Countries, rights domains, income standards, sex-disaggregated groups, and years; comparisons must respect the appropriate assessment standard and data availability.
observations.counterinterpretation: A low score may reflect measurement gaps, conflict, geography, or unusual service systems as well as policy failure; a high score does not eliminate unmet needs or future obligations.

denominator.unit: countries with at least one available right or component-right measure; exact coverage varies by year and domain

low_middle_income_composite.value: The composite SERF Index is available for up to 111 countries in any given year under the low- and middle-income standard

high_income_composite.value: The composite SERF Index is available for up to 28 countries in any given year under the high-income standard

component_rights.value: Component-right indices are available for up to 196 countries under the low/middle-income standard and up to 160 under the high-income standard, depending on right and year

interpretation.value: Global comparisons are strongest at the component level and weaker when reduced to a single composite score with uneven country coverage

observations.method: The update publishes composite and component indices with separate assessment standards and country-year availability determined by requisite data.
observations.uncertainty: Coverage is not uniform across years, rights, countries, or income standards. Missingness and data quality can affect apparent regional patterns and long-run comparisons.
observations.subgroup: Low- and middle-income countries, high-income countries, individual rights, country-years, and countries with modelled or look-back indicators.
observations.counterinterpretation: A component-right profile may be more informative than the composite and can reveal progress masked by missing data; the absence of a composite score is not evidence of poor fulfillment.

denominator.unit: countries covered by at least one relevant sex-disaggregated or component-right indicator

sex_disaggregated_domains.value: Sex-disaggregated data are included for education, food, two components of health, and one aspect of work under the high-income standard

rights_visibility.value: The update makes gendered differences in access and outcomes visible within a rights-fulfillment framework rather than treating country averages as neutral

work_dimension.value: The high-income standard includes sex-disaggregated data for one aspect of the right to work

interpretation.value: Rights delivery can be judged both by national feasibility and by whether access is distributed across sex groups

observations.method: The 2026 data update incorporates sex-disaggregated indicator and component-right data where internationally comparable measures are available.
observations.uncertainty: Sex-disaggregated coverage is incomplete and does not capture all relevant gender identities, intersectional groups, within-country geography, or causal mechanisms behind gaps.
observations.subgroup: Sex groups, income standards, rights domains, country income levels, and countries with adequate data.
observations.counterinterpretation: Disaggregation can reveal gaps but cannot by itself distinguish discrimination, household allocation, labour-market structure, health exposure, measurement bias, or different preferences.

denominator.unit: years in the updated international series, with country-right-year coverage varying

data_lag.value: The most recent available indicator and corresponding per-capita-income data are used; many underlying surveys are not conducted annually

lookback.value: Where modelled indicators are unavailable, the methodology can use a look-back period of up to 10 years; older data are recorded missing beyond that limit

standard_boundary.value: High-income and low/middle-income assessment standards are calculated for countries with required data but are not comparable to one another

interpretation.value: Global social-rights trend work requires explicit attention to data timing, modelled values, missingness, and benchmark choice before interpreting apparent progress or decline

observations.method: The project documents indicator recency, modelled inputs, look-back rules, missingness, and separate income-standard construction for the 1990–2023 series.
observations.uncertainty: Country-year scores may combine indicators from different years and data-generating processes. This limits precise timing claims and can make short-term changes look smoother or sharper than lived conditions.
observations.subgroup: Country-years, rights indicators, income standards, survey-based versus modelled measures, and regions with different statistical capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Long-run composite frameworks can still reveal persistent structural patterns that annual surveys miss, provided changes are interpreted as broad capacity/outcome signals rather than exact contemporaneous experiences.

related_sources.claim: Official announcement of the 2026 update, 1990–2023 coverage, five rights, country coverage, and sex-disaggregated data.
Official data and technical-note landing page for the 2026 International SERF Index update.

boundary: This record adds a rights-based delivery-versus-capacity measurement layer across health, education, food, housing, and work. It does not provide respondent-level data, a causal policy evaluation, a single comparable score for all countries, or proof that benchmark attainment means universal rights enjoyment.
